name: Krill oil

lead: Krill oil is an omega-3 supplement from Antarctic krill, with EPA and DHA carried on phospholipids and the carotenoid astaxanthin alongside. People take it for skin and general health, hoping less inflammation and a better skin barrier give calmer, healthier skin.

Several small trials report that it raises blood EPA and DHA about as well as fish oil, and the claimed advantage is better uptake. It is discussed for skin and inflammation, but no study has tested it for appearance. Fish oil has the larger outcome evidence base.

paras: It is taken as a daily softgel with a meal, usually as part of a general skin and health routine. Omega-3 changes build over weeks, and users often pair it with other skin-care habits.
Being crustacean-derived, it is not suited to shellfish-free diets. Krill research is newer and smaller than fish oil research, and harvest is regulated by CCAMLR.

angle.text: Krill oil is taken as a phospholipid-bound omega-3 source with astaxanthin: higher blood EPA and DHA are meant to lower inflammation and support the skin barrier, for calmer skin. It raises blood omega-3 in studies; skin effects are untested.

lead: Krill oil is a supplement extracted from Antarctic krill (Euphausia superba), a small crustacean. It supplies the omega-3 fatty acids EPA and DHA largely bound to phospholipids, along with the carotenoid astaxanthin, which gives the oil its reddish colour.[1][2] People take it as a fish-oil alternative for joints, lipids and general inflammation support, and for skin: omega-3s and astaxanthin are discussed as supports for skin hydration, a calmer complexion and slower visible ageing, and lifters take it for joint comfort and recovery that keeps training going.

It is compared mostly with fish oil, which carries the omega-3s mainly as triglycerides or ethyl esters. Several small trials report that krill oil raises blood EPA and DHA as effectively as or more than fish oil at lower stated doses, while fish oil has the larger body of outcome trials.[1][3][4][5]

A 2024 review in Frontiers in Nutrition surveyed existing studies on krill oil and skin, describing antioxidant and anti-inflammatory effects that it says give the oil potential in skin care and anti-ageing, and exploring the mechanisms involved.[6] Registered and published human trials of krill oil have focused mainly on blood lipids, joint pain, muscle and bioavailability. The product is sold worldwide, and the krill fishery that supplies it is a subject of sustainability discussion.
infobox: Manufacturer GRAS notices accepted by FDA[2]

paras: EPA and DHA together form roughly 20-30% of krill lipid fatty acids, and krill harvesting is managed by the Commission for the Conservation of Antarctic Marine Living Resources, according to Grokipedia. [1] Commercial harvest began with Soviet expeditions in 1961-1962. [1]

Wikipedia reports phosphatidylcholine, sometimes called marine lecithin, at about 34 g per 100 g of oil, and astaxanthin at 0.1 to 1.5 mg/ml depending on processing.[2] Krill oil is generally more expensive than fish oil, and Wikipedia notes that harvesting krill has been cited as an example of fishing down the food web.[2]

Krill oil is taken in softgel form for skin hydration, a calmer complexion and slower visible ageing, based on the antioxidant action proposed for astaxanthin and the anti-inflammatory role of omega-3s.[6] Some also take it to support joint comfort and recovery so that training volume can stay high, which indirectly supports physique goals.

Most human research has examined blood lipids and joint pain. A 2025 network meta-analysis of 39 randomised trials in knee osteoarthritis compared seven supplements, krill oil among them, against placebo.[7] Trials of krill oil in knee osteoarthritis include a JAMA randomised trial and a 6-month placebo-controlled trial in mild to moderate disease.[8][9]

sections.h: Krill oil compared with fish oil
paras: Krill oil carries much of its EPA and DHA in phospholipid form, whereas fish oil is typically triglycerides or ethyl esters; krill oil also provides astaxanthin and choline-containing phospholipids, and tends to cost more.[2] Proponents argue phospholipid-bound omega-3s are absorbed better, so a lower stated dose can reach similar blood levels.[4][5]

A 2025 review of EPA and DHA bioavailability in humans, covering fish, krill and microalgal sources, ranked chemical forms (free fatty acids and phospholipids above ethyl esters) but reported that differences seen in acute single-dose studies often did not carry over to chronic supplementation, and noted methodological limits in the field.[10]

A double-blind crossover study compared the incorporation of EPA and DHA into plasma phospholipids from krill oil and two fish-oil forms. [3] A trial in 113 people with normal or slightly raised cholesterol or triglycerides reported similar metabolic effects from krill and fish oil at a lower EPA and DHA content. [4] A four-week study reported a larger rise in the omega-3 index with krill oil than fish oil, and a study in overweight and obese adults reported higher plasma EPA and DHA after krill oil. [5][11] A mouse study found that DHA given as lysophosphatidylcholine, but not free DHA, increased brain DHA, and noted that standard fish and krill supplements do not. [12]

The 2024 skin review describes krill oil as containing n-3 polyunsaturated fatty acids, phospholipids, astaxanthin, vitamins A and E, minerals and flavonoids, and says its antioxidant and anti-inflammatory properties underlie interest in dermatology and anti-ageing applications.[6] The review draws largely on laboratory and animal work and on the wider omega-3 and astaxanthin literature.[6]

Krill oil also shows up in lifters' supplement stacks. Posts on T Nation describe taking it with fish oil, glucosamine and other supplements, and some users report using it for cholesterol management or alongside TRT.[13]

In rats, krill oil and fish oil matched for EPA and DHA differed in effects on ectopic fat and endocannabinoid-related inflammatory markers. [14] Reviews describe dietary omega-3 sources and fatty acid effects on hepatic steatosis. [15][16]

Bioavailability and lipid studies are summarised above.[3][4][5][11] A phase 3 trial of a krill oil agent with EPA and DHA as phospholipid esters and free fatty acids was run in severe hypertriglyceridemia,[17] and a multicentre JAMA trial compared krill oil with placebo for knee pain in people with knee osteoarthritis and effusion-synovitis.[8] A 6-month placebo-controlled trial in mild to moderate knee osteoarthritis was published in 2022,[9] and a 2026 pilot trial examined chronic musculoskeletal pain in older adults.[18]

Registered trials are testing krill oil for muscle protein metabolism, recovery after muscle-damaging exercise, sarcopenia, knee osteoarthritis pain, muscle weakness in type 2 diabetes and fasting triglycerides.[19][20][21][22][23] No clinical trial of krill oil on skin appearance, wrinkles or acne was identified.

Antarctic krill is a keystone species feeding whales, seals, penguins and fish. Wikipedia describes the krill fishery as on the order of 100,000 tonnes a year, taken mainly by South Korea, Norway, Japan and Poland and used mostly for feed and bait, and calls fishing pressure a growing concern alongside warming and shrinking pack ice.[24] Harvest is managed by CCAMLR.[1]
On T Nation, krill oil appears in lifters' logs and in threads on cholesterol and TRT, usually as one supplement alongside fish oil or in place of it.[13]

Krill oil is derived from a crustacean, so people avoiding shellfish are advised on labels to check products. Wikipedia reports that the US FDA has accepted manufacturer notices that krill oil meets generally recognised as safe standards, that it is on the EU list of authorised novel foods, and that toxic residues may be present in Antarctic krill and fish.[2] Harvest of Antarctic krill is regulated by CCAMLR.[1]

lore.intro: Krill oil is discussed in supplement and lifting forums as a fish-oil alternative, mostly for lipids, joints and general health rather than for appearance.[13]

Krill oil improves skin and slows visible ageing.
Krill harvesting is a sustainable source of omega-3.
